blocks.text: Reading on a phone is a different act from reading on a page. The eye travels shorter distances, the thumb sets the pace, and the screen asks for one idea at a time rather than a wall of paragraphs.

That is why audiobooks and reading apps have grown so quickly. People move between listening on a commute and reading in bed, and they expect the place in the book to follow them without any effort on their part.

A good converter treats a book as a sequence of ideas and pictures, not as a stack of pages. Pictures that explain something stay with the text that refers to them, and decoration is quietly left behind.
Consider how many people now split their reading between ears and eyes. The figure below shows the rise over the last decade.

blocks.text: Charts matter most. A reader who skips the chart often misses the point of the paragraph around it, so the chart must arrive at the same moment as the sentence that introduces it.
A book is full of images, but not every image belongs to the book. Logos repeat on every page, adverts interrupt the text, and borders decorate the margins. None of these should reach the reader.

blocks.text: Photographs are kept whole and scaled to fit a card, with the caption underneath. A reader can tap one to look closer, and a listener hears the caption read out in place.

A table of numbers reads badly as a picture, so tables are not turned into figures. The paragraph after it carries on as normal text, and nothing is lost from the argument.
